opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and it really comes down to the fact that most of our current language models are built on subword tokenizers like BPE, and those tokenizers are trained on a corpus that's heavily skewed toward English and a handful of other high-resource languages. So the vocabulary ends up being really well optimized for those languages. Common English words often get a single token, whereas a word in, say, Telugu or Burmese or even something like Finnish might get chopped into five, ten, sometimes more pieces, sometimes all the way down to individual bytes.

And that has very concrete consequences. If the same sentence takes three or four times as many tokens to represent in one language versus another, then you're paying more in compute to process it, you're using up more of your context window, generation is slower, and if you're using a commercial API that charges per token, speakers of those languages are literally paying more for the same service. There's been some nice work quantifying this kind of "token premium" across languages, and the disparities can be pretty dramatic.

Beyond efficiency, there's also a modeling question. When a word gets fragmented into units that don't line up with meaningful morphemes, the model has to do extra work to compose those pieces back into something meaningful. So the segmentation itself can make learning harder, not just more expensive. That's part of what motivates my interest in tokenizer-free or byte-level approaches. Byte-level models are appealing because they're more uniform across scripts and they avoid that vocabulary bias, but the catch is that byte sequences are very long, and some scripts need more bytes per character in UTF-8, so you can actually reintroduce a kind of inequity at the byte level.

That's where ideas like learned or dynamic compression come in, which is what we explored with MrT5. The idea is to let the model learn, inside the encoder, which byte representations it can drop or merge, so you shorten the sequence adaptively rather than committing to a fixed vocabulary up front. And what's interesting is that the model learns to compress different languages at different rates, in ways that reflect the structure of each language rather than a frequency-driven vocabulary built mostly from English. So for me the takeaway is that the tokenization unit isn't a neutral preprocessing choice. It bakes in assumptions about which languages are "normal," and if we want models that are efficient and fair across languages, we need to rethink that unit, ideally making it something the model learns rather than something we fix in advance.

r001.rationale: The response explains that some languages require several times as many tokens to represent the same sentence, increasing compute, context use, and generation time. It also describes language-dependent compression rates as a factor in efficiency differences.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because tokenization is one of those pieces of the pipeline that most people treat as a solved, boring preprocessing step, and it turns out to have really substantial downstream consequences, especially when you look across languages.

So the basic picture is that most modern language models use subword tokenizers like byte-pair encoding, and those tokenizers are trained on a corpus that's heavily skewed toward English. What that means in practice is that the vocabulary ends up being very well-suited to English. Common English words get their own single token, and you can represent an English sentence in relatively few tokens. But for a language that's underrepresented in that training data, or a language with a very different writing system or morphology, the same tokenizer has to break words into many more, smaller pieces. Sometimes you're down to individual characters or even individual bytes.

And that has a few consequences. The most obvious one is cost and latency. If a sentence in Burmese or Amharic takes three or four times as many tokens as the equivalent sentence in English, then a user of that language is paying more per unit of meaning, and the model is doing more computation for the same amount of content. There's also a context window implication, because you can fit less actual content into the same number of tokens.

But I think the more interesting consequence is what it does to the model's ability to learn. When you fragment a language into very small units, you're making the model work harder to reconstruct what the meaningful units are. The tokenizer isn't giving it any help. Whereas in English, the tokenizer has essentially already done a bit of morphological segmentation for free. So some of the performance gaps we see across languages aren't just about data quantity, they're partly an artifact of how we're presenting the data to the model in the first place.

This is actually part of what motivated some of the work I've done on moving away from fixed tokenizers entirely. If instead you operate on bytes and let the model learn its own dynamic segmentation, you remove this built-in bias toward whichever languages dominated the tokenizer's training corpus. The model can allocate its compute based on the actual information content of the input rather than on where the subword boundaries happened to fall. So I see tokenization as a real fairness and efficiency lever, not just an engineering detail.

r001.rationale: The response explains that the same meaning can take far more tokens in some languages, increasing cost, latency, and computation. This clearly identifies tokenization’s differing compression as a major efficiency factor.

astra-6.text:
I think tokenization is an important part of that, because the units a model processes don’t necessarily correspond to words, and they’re not equally granular across languages. A word in one language might be represented by a single token, while a comparable word in another language might be split into several tokens.

So if you’re measuring efficiency in terms of tokens, you have to ask how much information each token carries. Expressing the same thing in different languages can require different numbers of tokens. That affects how much text fits in the context window and how many generation steps the model needs to produce an answer.

The distinction I’d make is between properties of the language and properties of the tokenizer. If a language requires more tokens, that doesn’t necessarily mean the language itself is less efficient. It may mean the tokenizer’s vocabulary and training data give it a less compact representation of that language.

r001.rationale: The response calls tokenization an important part of efficiency differences and explains that different token counts reflect how compactly the tokenizer represents each language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think tokenization is an important part of that question, because a token isn’t a consistent unit of language. Depending on the language and the tokenizer, a token might correspond to a whole word, part of a word, or even just part of a character’s encoding. So the same content can require very different numbers of tokens across languages.

That matters for efficiency: more tokens means more computation to process the same message, and you use up the context window more quickly. It also complicates comparisons. If we train on the same number of tokens in two languages, we haven’t necessarily given the model the same amount of linguistic information.

So I’d distinguish the efficiency of the representation from how efficiently the model learns the language. Tokenization can introduce a substantial difference before we even get to the learning question.

r001.rationale: The response says identical content can require different token counts across languages, which changes computation and context use, and calls tokenization a substantial source of efficiency differences.
